item.title: How Universities Can Make Students Feel Like Impostors
item.description:
Imposter Syndrome

How Universities Can Make Students Feel Like Impostors

Universities are supposed to educate. But instead, they may impostorize.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Universities may unintentionally create the impostor feelings they try to help students overcome.
  • Students' impostor feelings may reflect their environments, not simply their own self-doubt.
  • Everyday academic practices and interactions can signal to students that they don't belong.
  • Before labeling students' feelings and fears impostor syndrome, consider they may actually be impostorization.

Whether you are a student in college or graduate school—or know someone who is—my hope is that reading or sharing this article will help students understand how our higher education institutions may trigger impostor feelings and what they can do to counter them.

University students walking.
Source: Sai Kiran Belana / Unsplash

Back in college, I remember walking to office hours to ask one of my professors a question. I was nervous. My palms were sweaty, and I was reciting what I would ask and say—everything from “Hello, Professor. I am a student in your class” to “I have a question…” This was the case every time I visited one of my professors. My biggest fear was that they would think my question or concern was silly and think to themselves, “How in the world did we admit her into this university?”

From an external perspective, I was a student experiencing impostor syndrome—which refers to feelings of inadequacy and a fear that others will discover that one is a fraud. Those who were quick to label my feelings as impostor syndrome assumed I suffered from low self-esteem or perfectionist tendencies.

But now, as a professor who has researched impostor syndrome for decades, I would not be so quick to label that nervousness and fear “impostor syndrome.” Those feelings were more reflective of impostorization.

Impostorization refers to the systems, dynamics, and interactions that lead people to question their intelligence, competence, and sense of belonging. Like many university students, I had worked hard in high school, earned good grades, graduated with honors, and believed I was ready for college. I was confident.

When I got to college, however, the confidence with which I had started began to diminish.

As I sat in large lecture halls, surrounded by people who looked nothing like me, I questioned whether I belonged.

As I heard professors comment, “This is basic,” “You should know this,” or “I’m going to go through this quickly since it’s likely something you have learned,” I questioned my competence. I did not know what they labeled basic or familiar.

As I sat in office hours, asking my professors questions while they continued typing and looking at their screen or the time, I wondered whether I was taking up space that was not mine.

As a first-generation college student and daughter of immigrants who had very little formal education and worked blue-collar jobs, I struggled to navigate a world that rewarded outspokenness, networking, and drawing on my family’s connections to land an internship or full-time job.

article continues after advertisement

College seemed like a playground that other kids were familiar with, while I experienced it as a place that was foreign and not created for people like me.

Whether intentional or not, there are various ways in which universities impostorize students and trigger the feelings typically labeled impostor syndrome.

University lecture hall with students.
Source: Tylijura / Unsplash

What is problematic with labeling students’ feelings of incompetence and unbelonging as impostor syndrome is that it assumes that the student is the issue rather than the environment. Workshops that focus on building students’ self-esteem and other skills will be of limited use when the context is what is triggering impostorism. An organizationally triggered issue requires an organizationally driven solution.

As students, we may have limited influence over forms of impostorization such as university policies, practices, and seemingly innocuous interactions, but there are steps we can take to help minimize their effects.

Identify the source of your feelings.

Are you feeling incompetent because of something internal (i.e., low self-esteem) or external (i.e., messages in the environment suggesting you’re incompetent for not knowing what others may know)? Different issues require different approaches.

article continues after advertisement

College is a bit tricky in the sense that everyone may be starting in the same classes, but not everyone is starting on the same foot. Some students come from high schools that had more resources and provided a stronger academic foundation than others. This is neither your fault nor a reflection of your potential. It just means that people like you and me must work harder and seek the support we need.

Go see your professors during office hours.

As a student, I remember feeling intimidated to go to office hours. But as a professor, I wish students would come see me so I may better support them.

My hope is that you will have the supportive and welcoming professors that every student deserves. But if you observe actions such as the ones I described earlier—i.e., professors looking at the time, preoccupied with their screens—please know that the issue is not you. Universities incentivize faculty to focus on research and publishing, often to the detriment of student learning and teaching. Seeking out professors is helpful not just in clarifying content but in establishing instrumental relationships—connections that may provide a sense of belonging in the classroom, job referrals, and letters of recommendation to support your future endeavors.

Share your feelings with someone you trust.

The impostor feelings I experienced were debilitating—they kept me from connecting with professors, asking for help, and embracing many of the opportunities offered to students. Once I started sharing with others how I felt, I discovered that I was not alone. I realized other people also feel inadequate and unintelligent, and question their sense of belonging in the spaces they occupy. It was reassuring to know that I was not the issue but the environment. The problem was not impostor syndrome but impostorization.

item.title: Is It OK for Your Partner to Have a Fetish?
item.description:
Sex

Is It OK for Your Partner to Have a Fetish?

Research says nearly half of us have a fetish, and most aren't dangerous.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Nearly half of adults report at least some interest in a sexual fetish.
  • Fetishes fall on a spectrum, from a mild preference to a core arousal need.
  • Sharing or accommodating a fetish is linked to greater relationship satisfaction.
  • Serial-killer cases are more likely to involve sadism, not just fetishism, which is rarely linked to harm.
Source: Kamaji Ogino/Pexels

Your partner mentions, tentatively, that a certain material, an item of clothing, or a specific body part does something for them that ordinary intimacy doesn’t quite match. Maybe you’re intrigued. Maybe you’re unsettled. Maybe your mind jumps straight to true-crime documentaries about killers with disturbing “collections.”

That reaction is understandable, but it’s also out of step with the research. In a large population survey, nearly 45 percent of adults reported at least some interest in fetishism, and roughly one in four said they had acted on it at least once. Fetishes, it turns out, are closer to a normal variation in desire than a red flag.

Not All Fetishes Are Created Equal

It helps to think of fetishistic interest as a spectrum rather than a single category. At the mild end, a fetish is simply a seasoning. It could be a particular fabric, scent, or piece of clothing that adds a spark to an otherwise conventional sex life.

Further along, the fetish becomes a meaningful and consistent part of how a person gets and stays aroused, something they’d genuinely miss if a partner refused to ever engage with it. At the far end, for a small minority, the fetish becomes compulsory. Arousal essentially doesn’t happen without it, and the interest can start to crowd out other parts of a person’s sexual and emotional life.

Clinicians reserve real concern for this last group, and even then, mainly when the fetish causes the person distress or involves someone who hasn’t consented. Most people who bring up a fetish with a partner are describing something much closer to the first two categories than the third.

Where Do Fetishes Come From?

No single explanation completely answers how a fetish forms, but a few theories dominate. The oldest is simple conditioning. Arousal that happens to occur alongside a particular object, especially early in life, can become linked to it.

In a well-known 1966 experiment, researchers were able to produce arousal in men simply by repeatedly pairing an image of a pair of boots with erotic slides. Other accounts emphasize that whatever cues happen to be present during formative sexual experiences can get woven into a person’s arousal pattern and stay remarkably stable for life. What’s consistent across these theories is that a fetish is something that happens to a person early on, not something chosen.

article continues after advertisement

A Little History of Fetishes

None of this is new. The word fetish comes from the Portuguese feitiço, meaning “charm,” once used for objects believed to hold spiritual power. Psychologists borrowed the term in the late 1800s.

For most of the twentieth century, the field treated any fetish as evidence of a damaged psyche. Freud, notably, framed it as a childhood defense mechanism. That view has aged badly.

Sex researcher John Money’s idea of the “lovemap,” the notion that everyone develops an individualized template for what turns them on, helped reframe fetishes as one normal variation among many, a shift now reflected in how the field diagnoses and treats them.

When a Fetish Helps or Hurts a Relationship

Sharing a fetish, or simply being willing to accommodate one, is associated with real relationship benefits. Couples in which partners actively engage with or embrace a fetishistic interest report higher relationship and sexual satisfaction than couples in which the interest is hidden or flatly refused.

This consistent with what sex therapists see clinically. Disclosing a fetish is an act of vulnerability, and a partner’s acceptance often deepens trust well beyond the bedroom. This doesn’t mean every fetish needs to become a shared hobby. It means curiosity and negotiation tend to serve couples better than silence, shame, or a flat “no” delivered without discussion.

Fetishes can also strain a relationship, and it’s worth naming when. Trouble tends to show up when one partner treats the fetish as optional spice while the other experiences it as essential, when a partner feels pressured to participate in something that doesn’t work for them, or when the fetish starts substituting for intimacy with the partner rather than enhancing it.

article continues after advertisement

None of that makes a fetish “bad.” It means that, like most things in long-term relationships, it needs honest conversation, clear boundaries, and ongoing consent rather than a one-time disclosure followed by silence.

About Those Headlines: Fetishes Aren't a Serial Killer Thing

It’s worth addressing the elephant in the room directly, since it’s the association many people carry into this conversation. Serial killer Jerry Brudos built part of his crimes around a shoe and clothing fetish, and true-crime media has run with that connection ever since.

But Brudos isn’t a window into fetishism generally, he’s an extreme statistical outlier in whom a fetish co-occurred with sexual sadism and a broader pattern of antisocial pathology. Forensic researchers who study these cases are explicit that fetishism itself isn’t the ingredient that produces violence, sexual sadism and antisocial traits are, and that fetishism occurs overwhelmingly on its own, with no connection to either.

The vast majority of people with a fetish—including, perhaps, your partner—are not a fetishism-plus-sadism combination waiting to happen. They’re people with a specific, fairly common turn-on who deserve better than a true-crime stereotype standing in for an actual conversation.

Conclusion

So, does your partner have a fetish? For nearly half of adults, the truthful answer is yes, but there is a strong chance you do too, whether or not you’ve named it.

What actually matters for a relationship isn’t whether a fetish exists, but whether it’s disclosed honestly, discussed without shame, and negotiated with mutual consent. Treat it the way you’d treat any other preference your partner brings into the bedroom, with curiosity first, boundaries where you need them, and the recognition that wanting something specific to feel good has never been the same thing as being dangerous.

item.title: Great Sexpectations: The Science of Good Sex
item.description:
Sex

Great Sexpectations: The Science of Good Sex

Everything you've learned about sex from the movies is wrong.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Human beings have always had sex, yet many of us still don't know what makes for good sex.
  • Social shame and reticence coupled with inaccurate media depictions skew our ideas of what makes good sex.
  • Science actually tells us how to maintain healthy and fulfilling sex lives over the long-term.

When it comes to what goes into consistent, sustained, and pleasurable sex, most of us have no clue.

If you believe what you see in the movies, you’ll think everyone but you is having spontaneous orgasms standing up in the shower. If you believe every headline you read in the news, you’ll think we’ve forgotten or forsaken sex all together. If you believe your pastor or tradwife influencer, you’ll think that if you're not having sex to make babies, you're morally depraved.

Like I said—perennially, tragically clueless.

As a philosopher, I spend a lot of time teaching people how spirituality is the pathway to alleviating sexual shame. As a scientist, I recognize that data helps. And when it comes to what makes good sex, science tells us much that we need to know.

Make it Play

A 2014 study found that sexual satisfaction has two main components: the individual’s positive feelings such as pleasure, arousal and openness, and the emotions that surface in relation to the other person—feelings like safety, compatibility and mutual attraction all create positive experiences.

But here's an interesting finding from that study: Couples interviewed revealed that orgasms were really not that important in the context of sexual satisfaction. Rather, intimacy and playfulness were big sub-factors. Intimacy includes closeness and connection, while playfulness indicates a level of comfort and vulnerability. Think about the last time you felt safe enough to play during sex.

Long-Term Lust

We tend to glamorize the early spark of a relationship and give into the inevitability of its demise. But a 2017 study dispelled this myth, revealing that it is possible to have fulfilling sex in a long-term relationship. In this study, couples that kept their mojo going past the honeymoon phase did more of the following:

  • Had more frequent sex (practice makes perfect)
  • Gave and received more oral sex (pucker up)
  • Had more consistent orgasms (there they are!)
  • Worked to set the mood (hello foreplay!)
  • Incorporated a variety of sexual acts (’tis the spice of life)
  • Engaged in frequent sexual communication—including praise, feedback and teasing

In short, you have to use your mouth.

Manage Your "Sex"pectations

In 2007, researchers put forth a theory of "Good Enough Sex" (GES) to help couples contextualize sex in a positive and realistic way into their lives. While sex is important for cementing a bond, reducing stress and for overall emotional and physical well-bring, the GES model recognizes that everyday life can get in the way of a healthy sex life. It urges couples to take the pressure off perfection and to acknowledge that variations in sexual performance over time are completely natural. Sometimes sex is mind-blowing, and sometimes it’s just “meh” and that’s totally normal.

article continues after advertisement

The GES model may seem to be pointing out the obvious—but in the absence of open and honest conversations around sexuality, people often internalize a lull in the quality or quality of sex as a personal failing. It's important to acknowledge that a fulfilling sex life is the result of a number of factors—mental, physical, and spiritual.

And as I always point out, sex doesn’t just happen between the sheets. It happens all day long, in and outside the bedroom. Technology can help you communicate better with your partner, can help you understand your own needs and boundaries, and can create a more adventurous and creative sexual environment. (Read my piece on how AI can make you a better lover.)

Now that you know the theory, go enjoy the practice.

item.title: The Empty Nest May Begin Before Your Child Leaves
item.description:
Parenting

The Empty Nest May Begin Before Your Child Leaves

Why do some parents start grieving when their child still sleeps down the hall?

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Imagining the impending separation can evoke feelings of sadness and anxiety.
  • Mental simulations may help parents think through uncertainties and prepare for challenges.
  • The anticipation of the empty nest can be worse than the actual experience of it.
Feelings of sadness might come even before your child packs their suitcase.
Source: Alexa / Pixabay

At the end of the summer, many families will be dropping their children off at college or university. There will probably be lots of big feelings: excitement and nervousness for the students, pride, sadness, and also nervousness for the parents. It’s a major change for everyone, but parents returning home to a quieter house may find the transition particularly challenging. Despite being excited about the adventure their child is embarking on, they may also experience their absence as a type of loss.

This transition is often called the “empty nest” phase. Parents’ experiences vary widely: some may feel sadness or loneliness, while others may feel a sense of relief or freedom. Some experience all of these at once. It’s perfectly natural to feel sad when the house feels emptier.

For some parents, though, the worry starts long before the car pulls away from campus. They may have been feeling it since the acceptance letter arrived. Of course they were excited about the news, and high school graduation was a reason to celebrate, but after that they may have been pre-emptively missing their child, even as they sat at the dinner table with them. They might have been feeling so nostalgic about every family outing—the last camping trip before college, the last family road trip, the end of the Sunday dinners—that they weren’t able to fully enjoy them. They might even have found their relationship with their child to be a bit strained because of this.

There’s a reason this can happen. When we know that an emotionally important change is coming, the mind doesn’t always wait for the event itself before responding to it. Instead, we construct mental simulations of the future, imagining what might happen and how it will feel. Research shows that imagining positive or negative events can influence mood, attention, and even behavior (Schacter et al., 2025). It can make the future emotionally present, resulting in feelings of sadness or anxiety simply at the thought of an empty bedroom or an extra space at the dinner table, even though the child is still at home.

There is a practical purpose to anticipating a difficult event. Imagining what might happen can help us plan and prepare for it in case it does happen (Schacter et al., 2025). In the case of a child moving out, the departure may be certain, but the consequences are not.

Parents may worry about how their child will adapt to their new school, whether they’ll make friends, and how they’ll manage academically. They may worry about safety, health, finances, or homesickness. They may also worry about themselves: Will their child still need them? How often will they talk? How might this affect their relationship with their spouse or other family members? This uncertainty can become a source of distress, because repeatedly imagining what might go wrong can make the coming separation feel closer than it is.

article continues after advertisement

Thinking about these questions ahead of time can help reduce some of the uncertainty about the future, especially if it leads to meaningful conversation. Making sure your child knows how to access supports, manage their finances, and ask for help when they need it can help them feel more prepared and you less worried.

It’s perfectly logical to have mixed feelings about a child leaving home. The transition may be difficult and stressful precisely because it represents something positive: your child is becoming more independent. A parent can be genuinely happy for them while also preemptively mourning the end of the family life they are used to. You can be proud of your child and also miss them before they have even left.

The good news is that the research suggests that the stereotypical image of the empty nest as an inevitable emotional crisis is misleading. A recent wide-ranging study examining the experiences of more than 40,000 parents, divided almost equally into those whose children had left home and those whose children were still living with them, found no differences in well-being and life satisfaction between the two groups: On average, the empty nesters were just as happy as the non-empty-nesters (Khreich & Ayoub, 2026). This doesn’t mean that the transition won’t be hard for some, but it does suggest that, at least for some parents, the anticipation of the empty nest might be worse than their actual experience of it.

It’s not always easy to stop thinking about the future, but there are things you can do that might make the transition easier. Try to get to the root of your anxiety. Is the main fear that you will miss your child? Are you worried about safety, communication, or your changing role in their life? Naming the specific concern can make it easier to respond to it.

article continues after advertisement

If you are worried that you’ll miss talking to your child, establish some expectations about how often you’ll connect with them. Negotiate this with them. How much are you both comfortable with? This might change over time, but it could make you feel better knowing that initially you can count on a weekly phone call with regular text check-ins. The goal isn’t to maintain the exact relationship you had at home; it’s to move into a new phase of your relationship that allows both closeness and independence.

Try to notice whether your anticipatory anxiety is keeping you from being fully present during the time you have left together. Savoring the remaining time doesn’t mean pretending things won’t be difficult. It just means allowing yourself to focus on the present.

If you are experiencing concerns about your child leaving home before they have even left, it doesn’t mean you are overprotective, needy, or controlling. It means you are facing a significant transition in a relationship that is important to you. You can be ready for your child to launch and not ready for the house to feel different. Both can be true.
